title: ERTH 209 practice exams
intro: Cumulative single-best-answer practice. Each question combines evidence, process, and interpretation from the course units.

tests.title: Cumulative Midterm Practice
tests.blurb: 34 challenging questions across Earth materials, tectonics, relative time, deformation, mass movements, and earthquakes.

questions.q: A coastline is quiet today, but its continental crust gradually changes into oceanic crust without crossing onto another plate. How should the margin be classified?
options: Passive margin within one plate
Transform plate boundary
Oceanic-continental subduction zone
Mid-ocean ridge
questions.why: A passive margin is not a plate boundary; the continental-to-oceanic transition occurs within the same plate.
questions.source: admin-only: ERTH 209 units on plate margins

questions.q: Oceanic crust near a ridge has thin sediment, symmetric magnetic bands, and becomes older away from the ridge. Which process best explains all three observations?
options: Seafloor spreading from newly formed ridge crust
Continental collision without oceanic crust formation
Transform motion that removes crust along the ridge
Hotspot activity beneath a stationary plate
questions.why: New crust forms at the ridge, records the magnetic field, and moves outward, collecting sediment as it ages.

img.alt: A ridge forms new crust that spreads outward with symmetric magnetic bands.

questions.q: A volcanic arc forms above a sinking oceanic plate, but the melting occurs mainly in the mantle wedge. Which explanation best connects the slab and the arc?
options: Water released from the slab lowers the mantle wedge's melting temperature.
The cold slab melts completely and rises as the arc.
The trench compresses air until it becomes magma.
Magnetic reversals heat the overriding plate.
questions.why: Volatiles released from the subducting slab promote flux melting in the overlying mantle wedge.

questions.q: A mineral scratches calcite but is scratched by fluorite. Which property is being used, and what range does this observation establish?
options: Hardness; greater than calcite and less than fluorite
Cleavage; greater than fluorite and less than calcite
Density; equal to calcite
Streak; darker than fluorite
questions.why: A scratch test compares hardness: the tested mineral is harder than calcite but softer than fluorite.

questions.q: Two samples have the same chemical composition, but one breaks along repeated smooth planes while the other breaks irregularly. Which property most directly explains the difference?
options: Cleavage reflects weaknesses in the crystal structure.
Streak records each sample's fracture pattern.
Hardness determines the number of crystal faces.
Lustre measures the sample's internal layering.
questions.why: Cleavage occurs along planes of weakness in a mineral's atomic structure; fracture is irregular breakage.

questions.q: A coarse-grained granite and a fine-grained basalt have similar overall silica-rich minerals. What most directly explains their different crystal sizes?
options: Granite cooled more slowly underground; basalt cooled more rapidly at or near the surface.
Basalt cooled more slowly because it erupted.
Granite contains no magma-derived minerals.
Crystal size is determined only by the rock's age.
questions.why: Slow cooling gives crystals more time to grow; rapid cooling produces finer-grained textures.

questions.q: A sandstone contains rounded quartz grains cemented together. Which sequence most plausibly produced it?
options: Weathering, transport, deposition, burial, and lithification
Melting, cooling, and crystal fractionation
Burial, foliation, partial melting, and eruption
Crystallization directly from a water-rich magma
questions.why: Clastic sedimentary rocks form as weathered grains are transported, deposited, compacted, and cemented.

questions.q: A metamorphic rock has aligned mica, and its mineral grains grow larger toward a nearby intrusion. Which interpretation best fits these observations?
options: Foliation reflects directed stress, while heating can raise metamorphic grade near the intrusion.
Foliation proves the rock formed from a lava flow.
The intrusion cooled the rock and reversed metamorphism.
Mineral alignment is evidence only of sediment deposition.
questions.why: Directed stress can produce foliation, while increased heat near an intrusion can intensify metamorphic changes.

questions.q: An undeformed sequence contains sandstone below shale and a volcanic ash layer above both. Which principle supports placing the sandstone earliest?
options: Superposition
Cross-cutting relationships
Faunal succession
Original horizontality
questions.why: In an undeformed sedimentary sequence, lower layers were deposited before the layers above them.

questions.q: A fault cuts a fossil-bearing bed but does not cut a younger ash layer above it. What can be concluded relative to those layers?
options: The fault is younger than the bed it cuts and older than the ash layer that seals it.
The fault predates both layers.
The ash layer must be older than the fault and the bed.
The relative order cannot be constrained by cross-cutting.
questions.why: A cross-cutting feature is younger than what it cuts; a layer sealing the feature is younger than the feature.

questions.q: A rock contains 25% of its original radioactive parent isotope and 75% daughter product. Assuming a closed system, how many half-lives have elapsed?
options: Two
One
Three
Four
questions.why: The parent fraction declines from 100% to 50%, then to 25%: two half-lives.

questions.q: A fossil species is widespread but existed for a short interval. Why is it especially useful for correlating separated rock layers?
options: Its short time range and broad distribution help identify equivalent intervals.
Its long time range proves every layer formed simultaneously.
Its presence provides an exact radiometric age.
Its location determines the original latitude of every rock.
questions.why: A widespread, short-lived index fossil can correlate layers deposited during the same relatively narrow time interval.
questions.source: admin-only: ERTH 209 fossils and stratigraphy units

questions.q: Fossils from two layers differ, but both occur in a long sequence of successive faunas. Which idea allows their order to be compared even when the layers are far apart?
options: Faunal succession
Isostatic rebound
Magnetic inclination
Metamorphic facies
questions.why: Fossil assemblages change through time in a recognizable order and can be used to correlate strata.

questions.q: A rock layer is tilted and folded, but its youngest beds are still on top when restored to their original orientation. Which principle supports that reconstruction?
options: Original horizontality
Uniformitarianism
Faunal succession
Isotope closure
questions.why: Sediments are generally deposited in near-horizontal layers; tilting and folding happened after deposition.
questions.source: admin-only: ERTH 209 stratigraphy and deformation units

questions.q: A rock layer bends without breaking under high temperature and pressure. Which description best fits the observed deformation?
options: Ductile strain producing a fold
Brittle failure producing an open joint
Elastic rebound without permanent change
Chemical weathering producing cleavage
questions.why: Ductile deformation bends rock into folds rather than breaking it along a fault or joint.

questions.q: A fault has a vertical component of displacement and the hanging wall moved downward relative to the footwall. Which stress regime most likely produced it?
options: Extension forming a normal fault
Compression forming a reverse fault
Shear forming a strike-slip fault
Heating forming a joint
questions.why: Extension commonly produces normal faults, in which the hanging wall moves downward relative to the footwall.

questions.q: A folded rock layer plunges beneath the surface and its map pattern closes in one direction. Which additional information is most useful for identifying the fold as an anticline or syncline?
options: The ages of the beds at the fold's core
The colour of the outcrop
The local slope angle alone
The current temperature of the rock
questions.why: An anticline generally exposes older rocks in its core, whereas a syncline generally has younger rocks in its core.

questions.q: A landslide moves as a coherent mass along a curved, spoon-shaped failure surface. Which classification is most appropriate?
options: Slump
Creep
Rockfall
Mudflow
questions.why: A slump is rotational movement of coherent blocks along a curved failure surface.

img.alt: Creep, slump, translational movement, and flow are shown moving downslope in different ways.

questions.q: After intense rain, a moving mixture carries mud, gravel, and boulders through a steep valley below a volcano. Which term best describes the event?
options: Lahar if volcanic debris is mobilized by water
Rockfall because all large fragments fall freely
Creep because the slope is wet
Lava flow because the material came from a volcano
questions.why: A lahar is a water-rich flow of volcanic debris; it is not molten lava.

questions.q: A hillside begins moving after a prolonged storm, although its angle has not changed. Which mechanism can explain the change in stability?
options: Water added weight and reduced resistance along a weak layer.
Rain removed gravity from the slope.
Saturation increased cohesion in every material.
The storm converted the soil into bedrock.
questions.why: Water can increase the driving load and lower resistance by saturating or lubricating weak material.

questions.q: A seismologist observes an abrupt change in seismic-wave speed at a deep boundary. Which inference is most defensible?
options: The waves have crossed into material with different physical or compositional properties.
The boundary must be the surface of the inner core.
The speed change proves all layers are liquid.
The observation directly measures mantle convection speed.
questions.why: Seismic-wave behavior changes at boundaries where material properties or physical state change; more evidence is needed to identify the layer.

questions.q: A region of continental lithosphere stands higher than nearby oceanic lithosphere. Which explanation best uses isostasy?
options: Differences in lithosphere thickness and density affect how the crust floats on the mantle.
Continental crust is denser and thinner, so it sinks lower.
Earth's magnetic field supports continents above oceans.
Oceanic plates have no lithosphere beneath them.
questions.why: Isostasy relates elevation to the buoyant balance of lithosphere with different thicknesses and densities.
questions.source: admin-only: ERTH 209 interior and tectonics units

questions.q: A sedimentary basin contains successive layers that record changing rivers, shorelines, and climates. Which approach best uses this record?
options: Interpret sedimentary structures and facies as evidence of changing depositional environments.
Treat each layer as a direct measurement of the modern environment.
Use only mineral hardness to reconstruct the basin.
Assume every layer formed at the same time.
questions.why: Sedimentary structures and facies help reconstruct the environments and processes that deposited the layers.

questions.q: A mountain belt shows metamorphic rocks, folded strata, and reverse faults. Which tectonic setting best explains the combined evidence?
options: Convergence and crustal shortening
A stable passive margin with no deformation
A transform boundary with only extension
A mid-ocean ridge with no compression
questions.why: Convergence shortens and thickens crust, producing folds, reverse faults, and metamorphism.
questions.source: admin-only: ERTH 209 plate-tectonics and deformation units

questions.q: A limestone is buried and recrystallizes without melting. What is the metamorphic rock called?
options: Schist
Quartzite
Marble
Phyllite
Gneiss
questions.why: Limestone is composed mainly of calcite; recrystallization during metamorphism produces marble.

questions.q: Which metamorphic rock commonly forms without foliation when quartz-rich sandstone recrystallizes?
options: Phyllite
Quartzite
Gneiss
Slate
Schist
questions.why: Quartzite forms from quartz-rich sandstone and is commonly nonfoliated; the other choices are foliated rocks.

questions.q: A geologist compares two clastic sedimentary rocks. Which property is NOT ordinarily used to classify their clasts?
options: Clast composition
Angularity
Colour
Clast size
Sorting
questions.why: Clast composition, size, shape or angularity, and sorting are useful classification properties; colour alone is not a defining clastic classification criterion.

questions.q: Which term is NOT one of the four broad sedimentary-rock groups used in the course?
options: Organic
Biochemical
Chemical
Clastic
Mafic
questions.why: The course groups sedimentary rocks as clastic, chemical, biochemical, and organic; mafic describes igneous composition.

questions.q: Ripple marks and dunes preserved in sedimentary layers are examples of which feature?
options: Bedforms produced by moving fluid and sediment
Foliation produced by directed pressure
Fault scarps produced by elastic rebound
Intrusive bodies produced by slow cooling
Index fossils restricted to one geologic period
questions.why: Bedforms are sedimentary structures shaped by moving water, wind, or sediment transport.

questions.q: Two earthquakes produce different maximum amplitudes on seismograms recorded at different distances and sites. Which conclusion is best supported by amplitude alone?
options: The larger recorded amplitude proves its Mercalli intensity was lower.
Its epicenter must be directly beneath the station.
The reading alone does not isolate source size from distance and local ground effects.
It must have been a thrust fault.
Its hypocenter was necessarily deeper.
questions.why: Recorded shaking depends on source properties, distance, wave path, and local site conditions; amplitude at one station alone is not enough to isolate magnitude.

questions.q: A seismograph records an early-arriving compressional wave after an earthquake. Which statement about that wave is correct?
options: It is a Love wave that travels only along the surface.
It is an S wave that cannot pass through liquid.
It is a Rayleigh wave with rolling surface motion.
It is a P wave that can travel through solid and liquid material.
It is a tsunami moving through the ocean.
questions.why: P waves are compressional body waves and can travel through solids and liquids.

questions.q: During a quake, the block above an inclined fault moves upward relative to the footwall. If the fault is shallowly dipping, which name is most specific?
options: Normal fault
Thrust fault
Strike-slip fault
Joint
Creep surface
questions.why: A thrust fault is a low-angle reverse fault, where the hanging wall moves up relative to the footwall.

questions.q: An earthquake ruptures the seafloor and displaces water across a broad area. Which wave property helps explain why the resulting tsunami can cross an ocean rapidly?
options: It is confined to the upper ocean and has a short wavelength.
It is generated only by wind and is driven by surface friction.
Its wavelength is long and the motion involves the full water column.
It breaks continuously as soon as it forms in deep water.
It is a shear wave traveling through oceanic crust.
questions.why: Tsunamis have very long wavelengths and involve the full depth of the ocean, allowing them to travel rapidly across deep water.

questions.q: A large earthquake damages two neighbourhoods differently: one is built on soft saturated sediment and the other on firm bedrock. Which process most directly explains stronger shaking in the first neighbourhood?
options: Elastic rebound
Strike-slip motion
Moment magnitude
Isostatic adjustment
Local ground amplification
questions.why: Soft or loose ground can amplify shaking; if saturated and loose, it may also be susceptible to liquefaction.
